title: The Man Who Made Himself
shortDescription: Given away at birth, adopted by a working-class couple, a college dropout who slept on floors and ate at a temple — he built computers in a garage, was fired from his own company at thirty, and came back to make Apple the most valuable business on earth.
introduction: On 24 February 1955, in San Francisco, a boy was born to two unmarried graduate students who could not keep him. His mother wanted him adopted by people educated enough to send him to college; when the first couple backed out, a machinist named Paul Jobs and his wife Clara, an accountant, promised to see him through university. That boy, Steven Paul Jobs, dropped out of that college, slept on friends' floors, collected Coke bottles for food money, and built computers in his parents' garage. At thirty he was fired from the company he had created. He came back, and built Apple into the most valuable company on earth. He made himself.

chapters.heading: The boy nobody claimed
paragraphs: San Francisco, February 1955. Joanne Carole Schieble, a graduate student from Wisconsin, had come alone to the city to give birth in secret. The baby's father, Abdulfattah Jandali, was also a graduate student, from Syria, and her own father had forbidden them to marry. She found a married couple willing to adopt her boy, but when they learned the baby was a boy they backed out. Stepping in were Paul Jobs, a machinist who had dropped out of high school and sold used cars, and his wife Clara, an accountant. They promised that the child would get to college no matter what it cost. On 24 February 1955 the boy was named Steven Paul Jobs and carried home to Mountain View, California — then a town of apricot orchards between San Francisco and the strips of land beginning to fill with electronics companies.

Steve grew up in a working-class home where the values were simple: work, honesty, and the resolve that he would have the schooling his parents never had. Around the age of twelve he decided his local junior high was a waste, announced he would not go back, and stuck to it until his parents sold their house and moved to Los Altos so he could attend the better Homestead High School. It was there he met Stephen Wozniak, an older boy with a gift for electronics, and it was on a neighbour's workbench that he first took appliances apart and learned to solder. Once, hunting for parts for a school project, he telephoned William Hewlett, the president of the electronics firm Hewlett-Packard, who was so amused he gave the teenager the parts and a summer job.

With Wozniak he built and sold blue boxes — illegal devices that let anyone make free long-distance phone calls — netting about six thousand dollars for a few months of work. It was a first taste of a lesson that would mark everything he did: technology he could help people feel was a kind of magic. And beneath the cleverness there was a simpler drive. He had been handed away once, and he said it plainly for the rest of his life — the couple who chose him were his real parents, and being chosen was what convinced him he could be worth choosing.

chapters.heading: Following his curiosity
paragraphs: In the autumn of 1972 Steve Jobs entered Reed College, a small liberal-arts school in Portland, Oregon, and majored in English. The tuition was high, and his parents were paying it from their savings. After a single semester he dropped out — he did not even tell his parents at first — because he could not bear spending their money on classes he was not sure he wanted. Yet he did not go home. For about eighteen more months he lingered around the campus, no longer enrolled, sleeping on friends' dorm-room floors and auditing whatever classes caught his eye: Shakespeare, modern dance, and a calligraphy course taught by a master penman named Lloyd Reynolds.

He had no money. He collected empty Coca-Cola bottles for their deposits and, he later told thousands of graduates, walked seven miles across town every Sunday night to get one good meal a week at a Hare Krishna temple. The calligraphy class he had fallen into taught him about serif and sans-serif typefaces and the careful spacing between letters — 'beautiful, historical, artistically subtle in a way that science can't capture,' as he put it. It seemed like study with no practical use at all.

In 1974 he took a job as a technician at Atari, a young video-game company in Silicon Valley, and saved his wages. Then, seeking something his textbooks had not given him, he and his friend Daniel Kottke flew to India to look for a spiritual teacher. They walked through a country where a barefoot man could survive on almost nothing, reached a mountain ashram in the Himalayas only to find its holy man had died months before, and returned from the trip changed. Back in California, wearing Indian cotton clothes with his head shaved, he took up Zen Buddhism, meditated, and kept asking the question that shaped his whole life: what did he, and no one else, want to build?

chapters.heading: The bedroom, the garage, the van
paragraphs: By 1976 Wozniak had designed a small computer circuit board for his own amusement — a machine a hobbyist could assemble and use. Jobs saw something Wozniak did not: that people would want this ready-made. He talked his friend into quitting his secure job at Hewlett-Packard to build the boards together, and on 1 April 1976 the two, with a third partner named Ronald Wayne, formed Apple Computer Company in the garage of Jobs's parents' house on Crist Drive in Los Altos — the first days actually operating from the bedroom. To raise money Jobs sold his Volkswagen minibus, Wozniak sold his programmable calculator, and the partners started with roughly thirteen hundred dollars. Ten days in, Wayne sold his tenth of the company back for eight hundred dollars; the other two would never have to share again.

The Apple I was a bare circuit board, but the Apple II, released in 1977, was a revolution sitting in a beige plastic case: colour, sound, and a keyboard, ready for a family living room. It arrived as computers were still giant machines locked in universities and government rooms, and it is the machine usually credited with launching the home-computer era. In January 1977 the partnership was incorporated as Apple Computer, Incorporated. On 12 December 1980 Apple sold shares to the public in one of the largest stock offerings since the Ford Motor Company went public in 1956. Jobs, who had just turned twenty-five, was chairman; his stake in the company was suddenly worth roughly two hundred million dollars on paper.

He was restless with what he had made. While Apple rolled out the Apple II, he poured attention onto a project called Lisa — named for his daughter — then onto a new, smaller, riskier machine he wanted to call Macintosh, a computer 'for the rest of us.' To run the company while he chased those dreams, he went hunting for a grown-up businessman and persuaded John Sculley, president of the soft-drink maker PepsiCo, to join him with a question that became legend: 'Do you want to sell sugar water for the rest of your life, or do you want to come with me and change the world?' Sculley came. The world was about to change; the friendship was not going to survive it.

chapters.heading: The machine that makes you feel
paragraphs: On 24 January 1984, Jobs stood on a theatre stage in Cupertino, California, and unveiled the Macintosh — the first computer many ordinary people had ever seen that you pointed at with a mouse and talked to with a screen that showed pictures as well as names. The Mac drew on ideas refined at Xerox's research laboratory at Palo Alto, California — windows, icons, a pointer — and turned them into something friendly instead of technical. The typography from his off-college calligraphy classes went straight into its fonts. To herald it, the company paid the director Ridley Scott to make a single, strange advertisement, shown publicly once during the American Super Bowl: a girl in running shorts hurling a hammer at a giant screen of a grey face, Liberty smashing Big Brother — a jab at the corporate computing giant of the day, IBM.

Jobs had not yet turned thirty when the press began calling him the father of the computer revolution. He ran the Macintosh team like a wartime general — brilliant, ruthless, and unforgiving of anything he considered a compromise. Colleagues gave his certainty a name: the reality distortion field, a refusal to accept that something was impossible until, often, it stopped being impossible. The Mac did not sell as fast as he hoped; it was expensive and unusual, and business buyers stayed wary. But the machine proved his deepest idea: a computer could be a thing a person loved.

The strain broke the company. Jobs, certain he knew better than the executives he had hired, tried to push John Sculley out; the board backed Sculley instead. In May 1985 the board stripped Jobs of his operating power. That September, aged thirty, he resigned from the company he had founded, sold nearly all his Apple stock, and went home to plan again. The outside world assumed it was the end of him.

media.alt: Steve Jobs sitting beside the Macintosh computer in January 1984
media.caption: Steve Jobs with the Macintosh, the computer that made friendliness a feature, photographed in January 1984.
media.credit: Bernard Gotfryd (Library of Congress) · Public domain

chapters.heading: The exile who built two more companies
paragraphs: The day he left Apple, Jobs sold almost all of his stock, and announced a new company he called NeXT, built to make computers for universities. The NeXT computer was designed with the same obsessiveness as everything he touched — a dramatic black cube with dazzling software — but the price was high and sales stayed small. What mattered most about NeXT, though, was its engineering, because that software became the foundation of Apple's operating systems for years to come.

A second gamble fell in his lap in 1986, when he bought the small computer-graphics studio Pixar from the filmmaker George Lucas for roughly ten million dollars. For years Pixar lost money while he quietly funded it and ran its business from the outside. Then, in late 1995, Pixar released Toy Story — the first feature film made entirely by computer — and its public offering of shares in the same season made Jobs, overnight, a billionaire again. In the same years he rebuilt his private self: he had a daughter, Lisa, born in 1978 to a woman he had initially tried not to acknowledge; a test proved she was his, and in time he supported her and grew close to her. In the mid-1980s, with the help of private investigators, he found his birth mother, and through her his biological sister, the novelist Mona Simpson. He chose never to meet his biological father.

In 1991 he married Laurene Powell, a Stanford business student he had met at one of his own talks, in a ceremony in Yosemite National Park conducted by an old Zen monk. They would have three children. Publicly, he admitted the cost of his own exile from Apple with a line that captured the decade: he told an interviewer in 1995 that he was probably the only person he knew who had lost a quarter of a billion dollars in a single year. It was true. It was also, as it turned out, the down payment on his return.

chapters.heading: Think Different
paragraphs: By 1996 Apple was in trouble: years without its founder, a string of failed products, and losses so deep the rumour was bankruptcy. In desperation the company bought NeXT for about four hundred million dollars — not for its computers but for its ideas — and its founder came back with it. The next year, 1997, Jobs agreed to run the company he had been fired from. First he bet again on the enemy: he asked Bill Gates's Microsoft, which Apple had just sued over a rival computer system, to invest a hundred and fifty million dollars in Apple and keep making software for it, and told his own customers they had to let go of the notion that for Apple to win Microsoft had to lose. The room booed the appearance of Gates on screen. Jobs pushed on.

Then he did the marketing that saved the name. The 'Think Different' campaign of 1997 showed photographs of the people he admired — Albert Einstein, Martin Luther King Jr., Mahatma Gandhi, John Lennon — with a text that called them the crazy ones, the misfits, the troublemakers, 'the ones who see things differently.' He had the audacity to list himself, without saying so, among them. In August 1998 the company shipped the iMac, a stubby, translucent-coloured computer that looked like a toy and sold brilliantly, pulling Apple back from the brink. By the year 2000 he had dropped the word 'interim' from his title and was simply chief executive.

The resuscitation lived on invented products: in 2001 Apple introduced iTunes, a music player that sat on the computer, the iPod, a small white box that promised a thousand songs in your pocket, and opened the first Apple Stores in real shopping streets. Each one owed its shape to a man who had learned, in a California garage, that a machine people could feel and love was worth more than a machine that merely worked.

chapters.heading: One more thing
paragraphs: In January 2007, at a theatre in San Francisco, Jobs stood up and said Apple was introducing three things — a widescreen iPod with touch controls, a revolutionary mobile phone, and a breakthrough internet communicator. Then he said it again, slowly, and it sank in: it was one device. The iPhone, with no physical keys and a screen that understood a finger, went on sale that June and rewrote what a telephone was. Caught unprepared, the old phone companies were left years behind; the screen, the app, the glass slab everyone now carries were born there. The iPad followed in 2010. Apple became the most valuable company on the planet — a company run by a man who had, a decade before, been worth nothing inside it.

In a final bow, the company that had once bought from him now merged with him: in 2006 the Walt Disney Company bought Pixar for about seven and a half billion dollars, and Steve Jobs, once an adopted nobody, became Disney's largest individual shareholder — a collector's sweep across movies, music, telephones, and computers that no businessman of his time matched.

The undoing was in his body. In October 2003 he was diagnosed with a rare, slow-growing form of pancreatic cancer. He delayed surgery for months, trying diets and alternative cures before accepting the operating room in 2004. In 2009, visibly gaunt, he took a medical leave of absence — later disclosed as a liver transplant in Memphis, Tennessee — and returned to launch more products as if illness were a design constraint he could manage. His body did not believe him for long.

media.alt: An original iPhone lying on a dark surface
media.caption: The original iPhone, the product that made Apple the most valuable company on earth.

chapters.heading: Stay hungry
paragraphs: In June 2005, when his cancer was known but his return triumphant, Jobs gave a commencement address at Stanford University that became the most-quoted speech of the digital age. He told the graduates three stories: about dropping out of Reed College and trusting that the scattered marks of his odd education would connect one day; about being fired from Apple, which he called the best thing that could have happened to him; and about death. 'Remembering that you are going to die is the best way I know to avoid the trap of thinking you have something to lose,' he said. He told them that their time is limited, so they should not waste it living someone else's life, and he ended with the farewell line of the last issue of a counterculture catalogue he had grown up on: 'Stay Hungry. Stay Foolish.'

He survived five more years. In August 2011 he resigned as Apple's chief executive — 'I have always said if there ever came a day when I could no longer meet my duties and expectations as Apple's CEO, I would be the first to let you know. Unfortunately, that day has come.' On 5 October 2011 he died at home in Palo Alto, California, aged fifty-six, of complications of the pancreatic cancer. The world's tributes came in nearly every language; on Apple's website for a week there was only a photograph of him and the years.

What he left was not the record of being given something, but of building it: the company he had been thrown out of became the most valuable in the world; Pixar changed how movies are made; the Ring campus Apple completed in 2017, the space-ship headquarters he planned and never saw finished, was renamed in spirit by the theatre at its heart — the Steve Jobs Theater. The moral of his life is plain almost to the point of defiance. He was handed away at birth, dropped out of the only road he was promised, and treated each rejection — by parents, by college, by his own board — as a door he was free to walk through and build behind. The man who made himself never once accepted an ending.
